title.en: Taiwan's Food Security in a Changing Climate

stages.source_description: Part 1: Introduction (Slides 1-3: hook on post-typhoon shelves, SDG 2 as food security, Taiwan's 30.7% self-sufficiency headline)

title.en: Thin shelves after a storm

A2.text: A typhoon hits Taiwan. Supermarket shelves look empty for a few days, and prices jump fast. Have you ever wondered what happens the next time?

B1.text: A typhoon can empty supermarket shelves within hours, and prices typically jump for a few days before finally settling back down again. But what happens the year that gap simply doesn't close?

B2.text: A typhoon can strip supermarket shelves completely bare within hours, with prices typically spiking for a few days before supply gradually stabilises. What happens, though, in the year that disruption simply refuses to resolve itself?

title.en: SDG 2 is food security, not just hunger

A2.text: SDG 2 is not only about hunger far away. It means food security: enough safe food, every day, for all of us. That includes Taiwan too.

B1.text: SDG 2 goes well beyond ending hunger in distant countries. It's really about food security, which means having reliable access to enough food every single day, for everyone in Taiwan too.

B2.text: SDG 2 extends well beyond alleviating hunger in distant countries. It's fundamentally concerned with food security, meaning genuinely reliable daily access to enough food, a standard that applies to Taiwan as much as anywhere else.

title.en: An island that eats mostly imported food

A2.text: Taiwan has about 23 million people. Most of our food actually arrives here by ship. In 2024, we grew only 30.7 percent of our own food.

B1.text: Taiwan is a crowded island with a population of roughly 23 million people. Ships transport most of what we actually eat. In 2024, we produced only 30.7 percent of our own food.

B2.text: Taiwan, a densely populated island of roughly 23 million residents, imports the majority of what it consumes by sea. In 2024, only 30.7 percent of domestic food consumption was actually produced here.

stages.language_pattern: present progressive for trends / this causes ...
stages.source_description: Part 2: Problem (Slides 4-6: self-sufficiency's 18-year low, grain vs rice gap, the hidden dependency at the dinner table)

title.en: An 18-year low

A2.text: That number keeps declining. It dropped to 30.3 percent in 2023, the lowest level in 18 years. It only rose a little after that year.

B1.text: That figure has been sliding for years now. It dropped to an eighteen-year low of 30.3 percent back in 2023, and it has only recovered slightly since that low point.

B2.text: That figure has been declining for years, rather than improving as officials once hoped. It fell to an eighteen-year low of 30.3 percent in 2023, recovering only marginally since that particular low point.

title.en: Rice is homegrown, most grain is not

A2.text: Look closer, and the picture splits. Rice is almost 100 percent homegrown here. But total grain self-sufficiency is only 25.5 percent. That's because most wheat comes from abroad.

B1.text: The picture changes once you separate the categories. Rice is nearly self-sufficient here, yet overall grain self-sufficiency sits at just 25.5 percent, since most wheat is imported from abroad.

B2.text: Breaking the numbers apart reveals a much sharper picture. Rice approaches near-total self-sufficiency, whereas overall grain self-sufficiency sits at merely 25.5 percent, given that wheat is almost entirely imported from abroad.

title.en: The hidden dependency on your plate

A2.text: So your rice grew here in Taiwan. Your bread almost never did. Even the pig that became your lunch probably ate imported corn instead.

B1.text: So the rice sitting on your plate has actually been cultivated here in Taiwan. That's unlike almost everything else you eat today. The bread beside it certainly hasn't, and neither has the cooking oil.

B2.text: So the rice occupying your plate was almost certainly cultivated domestically. The bread accompanying it, however, certainly wasn't, nor was the cooking oil in which it happened to be fried.

stages.source_description: Part 3: Achievements (Slides 7-9: rice production strength, the legal rice reserve, the Grand Grain Silo conversion plan)

title.en: Rice: a real national strength

A2.text: Here is some good news for once. Rice covers about 240,000 hectares of Taiwan. Two harvests a year produce roughly 1.21 million tonnes of rice.

B1.text: Rice remains a real strength for Taiwan. Across roughly 240,000 hectares and two harvests a year, farmers have grown about 1.21 million tonnes of rice recently.

B2.text: Cultivated across roughly 240,000 hectares in two annual harvests, rice remains genuinely secure here. About 1.21 million tonnes are produced every year, keeping this staple reliably available for everyone.

title.en: A reserve bigger than the law requires

A2.text: The law protects our rice too. Taiwan must always keep a rice reserve for three whole months. That target is higher than Japan's own goal.

B1.text: Taiwan has also written real protection into law over the years. A rice reserve must legally cover at least three months of national consumption, which sits well above Japan's own target.

B2.text: Legislative protection has also been established for this staple. A mandatory reserve, equal to three months of national consumption, is required by law to exceed Japan's own comparable target clearly.

title.en: The Grand Grain Silo plan

A2.text: Back in 2016, a new government plan actually started. People simply call it the Grand Grain Silo. It pays farmers well to grow soybean instead.

B1.text: Since 2016, a government plan called the Grand Grain Silo has paid farmers well across the island. It converts rice paddies into soybean fields instead of leaving good land idle.

B2.text: Since 2016, the Grand Grain Silo initiative has compensated farmers for converting rice paddies into soybean fields instead. This has gradually eroded decades of entrenched import dependency in the process.

stages.source_description: Part 4: Solutions (Slides 10-12: contract-farmed feed grain, feed-rice research, the cost trade-off of growing it here)

title.en: Turning idle paddies into feed grain

A2.text: Some rice fields used to sit unused after harvest. Today, growers can actually choose to plant corn there instead. That empty ground finally has a purpose again.

B1.text: Instead of letting abandoned paddies sit empty after harvest, farmers can now sign a contract to grow feed corn there. That turns unused land into a genuine, valuable source of grain.

B2.text: Rather than leaving idle paddies unproductive, farmers can now contract to cultivate feed corn there instead. This effectively converts otherwise wasted land into a modest yet genuine source of domestic grain.

title.en: Feed rice as a substitute crop

A2.text: Researchers here are also testing something quite new. They feed pigs with local feed rice instead of imported corn. It's a small step, but a real one.

B1.text: Researchers have also started testing feed rice as animal food instead of relying only on imports. This could make pig farming a little less dependent on a single imported crop.

B2.text: Researchers here have also begun trialling feed rice as a possible substitute for imported feed grain, for pig farms too. This work could gradually reduce reliance on any single imported commodity.

title.en: Self-sufficiency is not a free win

A2.text: But this is not a free win for anyone. Soybean grown here is far more expensive than soybean bought abroad. Someone always has to pay that extra cost.

B1.text: However, this clearly isn't a free win for Taiwan. A tonne of soybean grown here costs considerably more than one simply bought abroad, so someone still ultimately pays that difference.

B2.text: This is still not a free achievement, though. A tonne of soybean cultivated domestically is priced much higher than one imported from abroad, so somebody inevitably still absorbs that difference.

stages.source_description: Part 5: Implications (Slides 13-16: one throughline — efficient global trade vs. thin resilience when a shock hits both sides at once)

title.en: Buying cheap works, most years

A2.text: Farmers everywhere sell grain to the cheapest buyer. That is normal, and it works well most years. That is why almost nobody notices our heavy import numbers.

B1.text: Buying grain from wherever it happens to be cheapest works well in an ordinary year, most of the time. That's exactly why almost nobody notices how much of our grain is imported.

B2.text: Sourcing grain from whichever market proves cheapest works well enough in an ordinary, uneventful year. That's exactly why our heavy dependence on imports goes largely unexamined by the general public.

title.en: A quota that does not flex

A2.text: But global trade rules do not actually bend for us. Since 2002, Taiwan must import rice every year. That happens even when our own stock is already full.

B1.text: If a bad storm hits at home while shipping is delayed abroad, prices can increase quickly on both sides at once. Taiwan's own import rule still applies regardless of the timing.

B2.text: Global trade regulations, however, are not adjusted to reflect domestic circumstances. Taiwan has been obligated since 2002 to import a fixed quota of rice annually, regardless of how full domestic reserves already are.

title.en: How thin the buffer really is

A2.text: The buffer is thinner than it looks. Before Typhoon Krathon struck in 2024, vegetable prices jumped fast. They fell back only once the storm had passed.

B1.text: The buffer is thinner than it looks, too. Ahead of Typhoon Krathon in 2024, Taipei's wholesale vegetable price spiked hard, then eased back once the storm had finally passed.

B2.text: The margin proves considerably thinner than it first appears. Facing Typhoon Krathon in 2024, Taipei's wholesale vegetable price spiked sharply, only gradually easing once the storm had eventually passed through.

title.en: Efficiency and resilience pull apart

A2.text: So cheap imports keep our prices low most years. But they leave very little room for the year when trouble suddenly strikes twice, both here and abroad.

B1.text: So the same efficient system keeps grocery prices low most years. But it leaves little slack for the year a domestic storm and an overseas delay happen together.

B2.text: What this arrangement reveals is a system engineered for efficiency rather than resilience. It quietly sustains low everyday prices while leaving minimal slack for the year two disruptions coincide unexpectedly.

stages.source_description: Part 6: Call to action (Slides 17-20: two numbers at once, why STEM students decide the trade-off, a concrete ask, closing claim)

title.en: Two numbers, one island

A2.text: To sum up, Taiwan holds two numbers at once. Rice sits near 100 percent, almost every single year. Everything else sits near only 30 percent instead.

B1.text: To sum up, Taiwan really lives inside two very different numbers at once. It's nearly 100 percent self-sufficient in rice, yet only about 30 percent self-sufficient overall right now.

B2.text: In summary, Taiwan simultaneously holds two quite contradictory numbers at the same time. It approaches total self-sufficiency in rice alone, yet reaches only around 30 percent self-sufficiency across the entire food supply overall.

title.en: Why this is your trade-off to make

A2.text: This choice is not someone else's problem. Future engineers and farm planners will decide this. Maybe some of you will decide how much extra safety Taiwan buys.

B1.text: This trade-off matters directly to you. The planners who will decide how much extra self-sufficiency is worth paying for could easily be sitting in this very room today.

B2.text: This trade-off is one your generation stands to inherit directly. It is agronomists and engineers, quite possibly some of you, who will ultimately decide how much self-sufficiency is worth paying for.

title.en: Know where your food comes from

A2.text: So try this one simple habit. Think about where your dinner actually came from. Notice it whenever a new farm rule shows up online.

B1.text: So here's one concrete, practical ask for today. Pay attention to where your food actually comes from, and follow farm policy closely whenever new stories reach the news.

B2.text: So here is a concrete request worth seriously considering right now. Pay closer attention to where your food is actually sourced, and track agricultural policy as it surfaces within the news.

title.en: A full plate is not guaranteed

A2.text: A full plate today does not promise a full plate tomorrow. It never does. Let's not wait for an empty shelf before we finally ask why.

B1.text: Having enough to eat this year says absolutely nothing about what happens next year. So don't wait around for an actual crisis before you finally start asking these difficult questions yourself.

B2.text: Current abundance, however, offers no guarantee whatsoever regarding future supply. Rather than passively waiting for an actual crisis to strike, these difficult questions deserve to be raised well in advance.
